items.name: Readability
items.evidence: Mostly clear, but the Oracle-only `k.replace("%", "%%")` branch inside as_sql has no comment explaining why it exists. The generic name `transforms` sits next to `final_key`, and the copied `JSON_EXISTS(%s, '%s')` strings are not explained either.

items.name: Maintainability
items.evidence: The Oracle `JSON_EXISTS(%s, '%s')` SQL is copied into both KeyTransformIsNull.as_oracle and KeyTransformExact.as_oracle instead of using an overridable hook or subclass, which the conventions asked for. It also adds an unrelated vendor branch (`if connection.vendor == "oracle"`) to the shared as_sql.

items.name: Robustness
items.evidence: The `%` escaping is applied only to plain string keys, not to keys that come from a KeyTransform, so behaviour is inconsistent. The copied Oracle code also puts json_path straight into the SQL string. No errors are swallowed, and HasKey.get_prep_lookup handles None and expressions.

items.name: Array-index semantics kept for isnull / exact=None paths
items.name_zh: isnull / exact=None 路径保留数组下标语义
items.evidence: The final key uses `".%s" % json.dumps(str(final_key))` in the shared as_sql used by SQLite, MySQL and Oracle. Leading segments still go through compile_json_path. The isnull and exact=None paths now call `compile_json_path(lhs_key_transforms)` on the full path, so ints stay array indices there. It works, though by copying SQL rather than adding a subclass.
